newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stocks look stretched but reversal seen unlikely.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks look stretched but reversal seen unlikely.

text.p: The runaway rally in Hong Kong shares has left valuations stretched, but a serious reversal is unlikely, with favourable economic and political conditions spurring on the bulls, analysts said on Wednesday.
"Technically I think Hong Kong is a little bit stretched but fundamentally it is not," said Paul Guarnieri, director for the Asia Pacific region at Salomon Brothers Asset Management.

While the market may see a short-term pullback after rising some eight percent this month, analysts said steady interest rates, improving corporate earnings and confidence in relations with China, were providing a backdrop for higher prices.

The Hang Seng index overcame a bout of vertigo on Wednesday. The index tumbled 137.71 points during the session, only to soar again and close at a record high of 13,530.95, up 45.62 points, or 0.34 percent.

"It is a little dangerous to bet against Hong Kong immediately. I think it is going higher in the short-term just because of the momentum," said Gary Greenberg, deputy managing director at Peregrine Asset Management.
But he said the Hong Kong market was looking vulnerable. "It has discounted a lot of good news, most of it justifiably," he said. "In terms of valuation it is getting full."

Analysts said a correction on Wall Street would hurt the momentum in the local market. "We have got a fairly high degree of correlation between Wall Street and Hong Kong. It would be very difficult for Hong Kong to sustain its current performance if Wall Street starts to crash," said Guarnieri.
But analysts said the upward trend in Hong Kong was strong.

"The trend is still firmly up and all the indicators are still pointing up," said Alex Wong, technical analyst at Dharmala Securities. He said the market was showing overbought signals but only a drop below the 10-day moving average at 13,150 points would signal a pullback.
"It is still holding above the 10-day moving average. I think the market is still likely to go up and it is too early to pick the top," he said.
Analysts said investors had a friendly interest rate environment to look forward to going into 1997.

Earnings growth of about 15 percent in 1997 and expectations of a smooth handover of Hong Kong to Chinese rule in mid-1997 would also keep the index moving up, said Jake van der Kamp, investment strategist at HG Asia.
"I can't see a correction at these levels. I still think it is worthwhile buying this market," he said.

Van der Kamp said political and economic factors were prompting investors to discard traditional price earnings (PE) multiples. He said a Hang Seng at 15,000 points could be sustained throughout 1997.

Research analyst at Mansion House, Henry Lui, said: "If you look at the PE it is just under 13 times (1997 earnings) so it is really not expensive compared to the peak of 22 times when the market crashed in 1987."

Gilbert Chu, head of research at Crosby Securities, said the market could reach a PE of about 14 to 15 times by the end of 1997, with the Hang Seng trading between 16,000 points and 18,000 points by the end of next year.
